title: A Portable Benefits Pilot for NYC’s Growing Freelance Creative Workforce
plain_title: Portable benefits pilot for New York City freelance artists
what_they_audited: A report from the Center for an Urban Future examining how the rise of freelance and self-employed work is changing the economic realities facing New York City's artists and what policymakers can do about it. It draws on new analysis of employment and Census data, interviews with artists and experts, and a review of emerging portable benefits models.
background: The report says the number of artists living in New York City grew nearly 35 percent from 2004 to 2019, then fell 4.4 percent from 2019 to 2024. It says employment across the city's creative industries is also down about 6 percent from before the pandemic.

findings.plain: Self-employment in the creative economy has grown since 2019 even as overall creative employment shrank, and it is growing faster than self-employment citywide.
findings.quote: Since 2019, the number of self-employed creative industry workers has risen 12 percent—nearly four times the 3.1 percent growth in self-employment citywide—even as the creative economy shrank overall.

findings.plain: Self-employment is far more common among creative-industry workers than among private-sector workers citywide, and the shift spans most creative occupations.
findings.quote: Of the 27 occupations we tracked, 23 saw an increase in self-employment since 2019.

findings.plain: Self-employed creative workers earn less than wage-employed workers, even when working full time.
findings.quote: Full-time self-employed workers in creative occupations earn a median of $60,000 a year, 34.1 percent less than full-time wage-employed workers ($91,100).

findings.plain: Artists have gaps in health coverage and employer benefits, based on a survey by Creatives Rebuild New York and other sources cited in the report.
findings.quote: A recent survey by Creatives Rebuild New York found that 18.4 percent of New York City artists lack health insurance

findings.plain: Self-employed creative workers are more likely to rely only on public health insurance, which leaves them more exposed when public coverage is cut back.
findings.quote: Fully 25 percent of self-employed workers in creative occupations rely exclusively on public coverage, compared with 9.3 percent of wage-employed workers in the same jobs.

findings.plain: Freelancers describe handling taxes, insurance and benefits across many projects as a job in itself, and some say the lack of benefits affects career and family decisions.
findings.quote: “When you are freelance, you have to find work, do the work, and also be your own accountant and HR,”

recommendations: Launch a portable benefits pilot for artists and creative workers so independent workers keep essential benefits as they move between gigs, employers and sectors.
Use a pooled social insurance model rather than individual savings accounts, so workers share risk and the group has more leverage to negotiate affordable coverage.
Draw contributions from multiple sources, including employers, clients, philanthropy, individuals and the public sector.
Set eligibility rules that reflect freelance work, including fluctuating income and workers who receive both W-2 and 1099 income.
Design the legal and regulatory structure to protect participating employers from unintended tax liabilities or worker-misclassification penalties.

Involve state government to help provide funding and address regulatory questions the city cannot resolve on its own, particularly around insurance, taxation and the treatment of employer contributions.
Make enrollment simple and easy to navigate, and design it to reach workers across the creative sector, including those who have historically had little access to benefits infrastructure.
Include a clear evaluation plan from the start so the city can track results, fix problems and identify what it would take to scale the model.
